She still feels the effects of being shaken and warns her: another time, if I do not answer while I am praying, do not disturb me. She asks her to look for a flat to rent for a month for Carlotta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hope you had a good journey and have already done a lot of work;2 yesterday I did not write because I was left with a trembling that made it impossible to hold the pen.

2. Oh! how I suffered when you shook me.3 Oh! It is clear that my dearest daughter does not know me yet. Ah! daughter! for pity's sake, another time, if I do not answer, do not disturb me!4 I have only the night; by day I am always in the midst of business.5 Enough! I will say no more.

3. Listen, Carla and Gaspare send greetings; they arrived yesterday at half past two; I tell you nothing about the Father, because yesterday morning he went to S. Lazzaro.6

4. I am anxiously awaiting your news; it seems a hundred years since I saw you; hurry! Today I have nothing to tell you.

5. Listen, see whether you can find cheap lodgings for Carla for just one month; you can ask your sister, whoever you think, Alessandro, but I would not want them to go to the aunt's house.7 If all else fails they will go there; meanwhile see what they would ask for a month. That way they will give nobody cause for talk, isn't that so? Goodbye, your more than affectionate and eternal Mother

affectionate M. R.

1 The date is deduced from the context, and in particular from M. Rosa's L 409, with

the remark: yesterday I wrote to you.

2 Sr. A. Benedetta had gone to Genoa on 5 November to visit and reorga-

nize the houses in Genoa, Sampierdarena and Sestri Ponente.

3 How I suffered when you shook me. On the evening before leaving, Sr. A.

Benedetta, entering the Mother's room and finding her absorbed in prayer and un-

responsive to her voice, had shaken her.

4 If I do not answer, do not disturb me. Sr. A. Benedetta answers: "Yes,

alas, the night hours all belong to your Crucified One. But forgive me for having

been so cruel as to take you from him... it will never happen again".

5 An expression that sums up her life, wholly given in love to God and

neighbour. A love drawn from its source, her Crucified Beloved, in intimate contemplative

attraction during the night, and poured out in action for her brothers and sisters in the

midst of business by day.

6 It is Fr Tornatore.

7 Aunt Emilia, sister of her mother Adelaide. Cf. L 267, n. 1.

She gives news of her own health and of Father Tornatore. She urges her to obtain the decoction for the Cardinal Protector.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter, mine for ever,

1. Yesterday I wrote to you and I also received your letter telling me to send to the station for the decoction for the Father.2 Listen, so far nothing has been seen.

2. Listen, for pity's sake take care of yourself; I am well, and the news brought me yesterday of the Father, who is at S. Lazzaro, is good: he seems a little better, the decoction has done him good; I hope the other will arrive. Tell Mrs Maddalena that for pity's sake she must not let the Cardinal run short of it.3

3. Goodbye, I have so much to write that I really don't know how to manage; they want answers from all sides. Goodbye, yours for ever, eternally

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 Through an oversight this letter is dated October. It is in fact from No-

vember, as the context clearly shows.

2 Fr Tornatore was unwell and was taking the decoction prepared by

Mrs Maddalena Bacigalupo.

3 The Cardinal Protector Giuseppe Berardi used Mrs Mad-

dalena's decoctions, but she was rather reluctant to supply them, offended by his generous

offer of money. (Cf. L of 8.11.77 from Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega to M. R.).

She gives news of her own health, of Carlotta and family, and of Fr Tornatore. She asks her to thank Mrs Maddalena.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Last night I received yours and hear what you tell me about the Genoa house;1 I can see it is a hard fight with people set in their own ways. Enough, let us hope the Lord puts it right.

2. I am well, and so are the little doll,2 Carla and Gaspare. Carla grows plumper every day, you will see her; tell Mrs Maddalena too that she is really well and is already beginning to feel better; the Father is better, but his head is always buzzing;3 tell her, so that she will send him something to cure him quickly; he is still at S. Lazzaro.

3. I hope you will soon be able to finish everything and come to me, for it seems a hundred years that you have been away. So, patience for Jesus' sake; one day we shall never be parted again.4

Yours in haste,

your affectionate M. R. GATTORNO

1 She has received the L reporting the reprehensible conduct

of some Sisters.

2 puppa: little doll, the pet name of little Maria Adelaide, Carlotta's first

daughter.

3 Fr Tornatore is better; his head is always buzzing: a Genoese expression

meaning: he hears a ringing in his ears.

4 we shall never be parted again. The sense of eternity, very much alive in M. Rosa, surfaces

often and in various expressions, according to the circumstances of daily life.

She should accept the Postulant. She thanks her for what she has done for Alessandro. She should tell Mrs Maddalena of the good effects of the decoction. Some instructions.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Here I am, all yours; whatever will you have said about my never answering your question about the Postulant?1 I really am a dunce: I would sit down to write to you meaning to do it and instead always forgot; well then, accept her, and so she can come with you; what do you say?

2. I hear about Mamma; patience is needed.2 Alessandro writes to me that you are being a mother to him and that you have given him his chain.3

3. Oh! dear Benedetta! What am I to do for you? You will see that the charity you show me will certainly not be in vain, nor will you be disappointed, I hope. Ah! If my God will hear me, ah! my daughter will be at my side for all eternity.

4. Listen, yesterday the Father wrote to me that he is a little better and owes it to the decoction,4 but he has none left and asks her to make something to take away the heat he still has, though he is much better; so tell her,5 and also if she could see Carla, how she fattens up every day. I took it, but it did nothing for me; but I hope it did me good all the same, because it always does good.

5. Tell Alessandro that I don't think they want it, so he should leave it all open; you'll see it is better; they don't want to spend money.6 Goodbye, I am your

Affectionate M. R. 609

6. I have received the baskets; if you have no money for the journey, write and I shall send it.

7. Tell Alessandro to keep the 150 f.,7 and I would like to know whether Fr Accinelli has hopes of collecting the little still due to me from my brother-in-law, and whether he has had the Parish Priest summoned, and if he thinks of leaving with the two he mentions, let him go, he will do well; that way he will get to the bottom of everything.8 Goodbye

[your affectionate M. R.]

1 On 6.11. Sr. A. Benedetta had written to her that a Postulant had applied

and gave her good references.

2 I hear about Mamma. Given her age (75) she had her fads (cf. L of 8.11. from Sr. A.

Benedetta to M. Rosa) and made herself unhappy and difficult: "Poor woman, I feel

sorry for her, being such a victim of her own ideas"!

3 You have given him his watch chain. Perhaps it had been pawned.

4 Cf. L 410, n. 3; 409, n. 2.

5 Tell Mrs Maddalena, giving her precise reports on the effectiveness or

otherwise of her preparations.

6 She refers to the flat Alessandro had found and rented for a month for his sister Carlotta. Cf. L 408,5.

7 This is the money paid in advance as a deposit on the above rent.

8 and I would like to know... the bottom of everything. She asks for news about some matters in hand

that Fr Accinelli was dealing with, namely:

- whether he had collected the small sum (the little) that her brother-in-law Vittorio Custo owed his nephew and niece Carlotta and Alessandro as interest on their paternal grandmother's dowry;

- whether he had served the summons on the Parish Priest Fr Giovanni Boffetti concerning Sr. A. Teresa's dowry, which he was illegally withholding;

- if he thinks of going to Novara to see the said Parish Priest together with Sr. A. Teresa and Sr. A. Serafina (the latter was entitled to a small annual income, also held by the Parish Priest), let him go, and so everything will be cleared up.

Since she is unwell and cannot solve the houses' problems so quickly, she tells her to return to Piacenza. She will go back to Genoa with her later. Meanwhile she should pay the Vernengo sisters.

A.M.F.

My dearest daughter,

1. Listen, this is what I would do, because from your letters I see that you are not well and are taking things too much to heart.1 Listen, let us do it this way: come, leave things as best you can, and then we shall go back together; by then they will be in the new house2 and I shall also go to S. P. d'Arena.

2. Tell Fr Accinelli that instead of his coming here, I shall come there before he leaves for Rome.3

3. As for the money, I think that in all, he wrote to me, it came to 26,00 F.;4 now, for the Vernengos, give him the postulant's 400 fr., and as for mine, find out whether the tenant farmer5 has already paid this year; if he has not yet paid, let me know.

4. Oh! Dear daughter, come soon, and meanwhile we shall go back together. I am not sending him the two thousand, because he will certainly take Sr. A. Teresa's;6 so it seems pointless to me, doesn't it? Come soon; the rest in person.

Your affectionate M. R.

1 Cf. Letters of 11 and 13 November 1877 from Sr. A. Benedetta to M. Rosa.

2 the new house. Fr Accinelli was preparing a new, larger home for the Genoa

community.

3 Mother Rosa's departure for Rome around Christmas was being planned.

4 Fr Accinelli had written to her that she owed him L. 2341 for expenses incurred

on behalf of the Institute and L. 604 for administering Mother Rosa's affairs. The Vernengo sisters

were owed a quarterly annuity. Cf. L 14, IL 2.

5 The tenant farmer: the sharecropper who worked the garden of the Sampierdarena house.

6 Cf. L 411, n. 8.

She rejoices that the House is going well. She will let them know when they are to come to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste: I have received your letters and am extremely pleased that your House is going so well. God keep you. Listen, if I do not write it is for lack of time and because I am always unwell;1 tell Sr. A. Sempliciana so; when you are to come, it is best for you both to come together; I shall telegraph you: Come at once.2

Goodbye, your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The Superior wanted news of the Mother.

2 Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti, like the Superior, hoped to go to Piacen-

za to meet her. Cf. L 417,2.

She invokes God's blessing on the schools just begun. Encouragement and spiritual advice.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear the good news you give me.1 Oh! God bless the schools you have begun! Yes, my dear daughter, whoever keeps her thoughts turned to God and her gaze always on the prow, which is our superiors, may be sure that the ship (you) will always reach a safe harbour.

2. I hope the municipal schools2 will be well paid, and so you will be comfortable.3

3. Yes! The days fly by and soon we shall see each other. Oh! What fine things we shall tell each other about the Lord's Work! So let us compete to see who works hardest. Courage and love of God in all things. Charity towards your neighbour, self-denial, and you will have all you desire,4 your

Affectionate M. R.

1 the good news: the Bishop has assigned a chaplain who will celebrate

Mass every day free of charge; they have obtained the Province's subsidy for

the "Sunday school"; the municipal school has opened with 40 pupils; five gi-

rls have applied to enter the boarding school. Cf. L of 14.11.77 to M.

Rosa.

2 The municipal schools too had been entrusted to the FSA. Cf. L 393,3.

3 comfortable: financially secure.

4 These are evangelical values distinctive of the being and acting of the FSA.

She charges her with sending the Sisters off to Foligno and Spello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. As soon as you receive this, send Sr. A. Olga at once to

Foligno;1 she can go together with Sr. A. Gennarina if she has not yet

left; if not,2 try to have her accompanied by someone

else who could act as cook for the hospital at Spello.

2. Write to me at once; in haste, I say no more.

Goodbye, your

affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Olga Tornelli, a teacher, was expected at Foligno, as was Sr. A. Genna-

rina Lovisolo.

2 ...if not: otherwise...

The Sisters delivering this letter are to leave for Naples.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I reply to yours about the piano.2 Yes, do buy it, I am delighted; that way it will be yours.

2. I hope the Cardinal will send me something for the raffle.3 These Sisters are for Naples and you are to send them on at once; if you think fit, let them see the Pope.4 Have you not enquired about the rent?5 I think it is already due. Goodbye, your

Affectionate M. R.

1 The date is deduced from the content and context of the correspondence of the

time.

2 Piano lessons were given in the Vicolo Margana House. The

Superior had found a good opportunity to acquire one. The raffle under way in Piacenza. Cf. L 403,2. It was easy to obtain an audience with the Holy Father. The house rent was paid in two half-yearly instalments.

She is glad the municipal authorities have raised the Sisters' salary, but it is still inadequate. They should refer to her for further decisions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I receive your two letters; I am very pleased with the good news you give me about the increase, but it is still too little.1

2. Tell Sr. A. Sempliciana that I expect her for Christmas Eve, so she will spend the feast with me and we shall understand each other better in person.2

3. Listen, you say you are sending me a document, but you sent me nothing.3 If these Gentlemen want anything, tell them to apply to me, for you cannot give any answer; do you understand?4

4. For the rest I am delighted. God bless you; I hold you close in the heart of Jesus as my dear daughters, and I leave you with my pen but am always with you in thought; I am your

affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti (the teacher) and the Superior had written to her on

8 December. The latter had given her the good news of the increase in

salary for the three teaching Sisters.

2 The Sister thus has her wish to see the Mother and speak with her granted.

3 The Superior had written that she would send her the resolution on the

salary increase once it had been implemented.

4 if these Gentlemen: the Mayor and the town Councillors.

She explains the difficult situation created in the Palagano community and in the town by the lay teacher, who has put the Sisters in a bad light and had herself appointed teacher, excluding them from the school.

[Most Reverend Excellency,]

1. Trusting in the immense charity Your Most Reverend Excellency has always shown towards this poor Institute, I venture to write to inform you of certain disorders occurring in our House at Palagano, without concealing from you the cause of all the trouble.

2. Your Most Reverend Excellency knows how well that House was going and how pleased everyone there was, because the Sisters, by the Lord's grace, had won the love of their pupils and the esteem of the whole town.1 Some months ago Fr Giovanni Brugioni came to see me in Piacenza; he repeated in person all the praise he had given me countless times in writing, and before leaving told me he wished to consolidate that House and put various plans to me for doing so.

3. I replied that I left everything in Your Most Reverend Excellency's hands, adding that for me it was enough that the sisters should have enough to live on.2 These proposals of Fr Giovanni show how satisfied he was with our work, and the whole town with him.

4. But now things have taken a different turn, and here is the cause. I let myself be persuaded to send there a lay teacher who had entered our Institute intending to become a Religious, and whom I did not want to clothe before sending her to Palagano, intending to test her vocation to the religious state. I sent this teacher there because she had come to me recommended by the Daughters of Charity, indeed brought here by them, and because, as she also knew French, I thought her very suitable for teaching those boarders and

pupils.

5. But the result did not match expectations. The teacher, who at first seemed a lamb, has now risen up against us and, sowing discord by dint of slander between the Superiors, among them Fr Giovanni, and us, has managed to have herself appointed teacher in title, taking the school from us. I do not wish to characterize this action, for charity does not allow it; but it is certainly neither good nor honest.

6. Oh! If you could see from a letter of Fr Giovanni's how much he has changed in a few months from what he was before, you would certainly be convinced that some wicked person is at work. The persecutions will cease there too, I hope, but at present they exist, and very strong ones.3

7. I have informed Your Most Reverend Excellency of this because, while I care little about losing the Palagano House, which, as Your Excellency knows, has cost me immense sacrifices, I should be very sorry to lose the esteem and goodwill with which Your Most Reverend Excellency, in your immense charity, has always been so generous towards us poor Daughters of Saint Anne. Prostrate at your feet and invoking your Pastoral Blessing, I declare myself Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The House had opened in 1875.

2 For me it was enough that the Sisters had enough to live on.

3 The teacher left. Cf. L of 24.12. and 29.12.1877 from the Superior Sr. A. Euge-

nia Gaudenzi to M. Rosa.

If she can, she should send the Sisters' money, as she needs it. She asks for information on whether a Sister of the Community is fit to be Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I receive your letter and hear about Sister A. Natalina's money;1 if you can, it is better for you to send it here to me, for I always need it. Oh! Would to God I could have it! May the Lord's will be done in all things.

2. I am extremely sorry about the Duchess's health; pray, for pity's sake.2 The consolation of hearing of the good being done gives me the greatest pleasure. God bless you together with the sisters, and believe me yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

3. P.S. Listen, I would need you to give me your frank and clearly stated opinion of Sr. A. Marziale, whom I would like to make Superior in a school where there are only 4 sisters with her.3 What do you say, since you have had her with you for a long time?

4. Listen, for the school I shall send you another good one. What do you say? Answer me at once, for I need it, but in complete secrecy.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Natalina Armillei had inherited L. 100 from her relatives.

2 The Duchess Agnese of Sora Piombino, a great benefactor of the Institute.

3 Sr. A. Marziale Mola. Sr. A. Guglielma's opinion is well weighed: "if

she wishes, she could be very capable; true, she is still a bit girlish now, but

when she has responsibilities I hope she will no longer be so; let us hope she will do well".

She acknowledges receipt of the money.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Just a line: I have received the money, thank you,1 and also for the information you give me about the Sister.2 God give his Holy Blessing to you all, and to you in particular. Believe me your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 She has sent her the money mentioned in L 419,1.

2 Cf. L 419,3 and the related note.

She encloses the letter of a Sister's mother, worried that her daughter has not written.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received this very insolent letter from the mother,1 as you will see; let her read it and then tell her to answer it herself, for I will not answer and cannot understand why she has written to me in such terms; enough, she must defend herself; I am writing nothing.2

2. In the hope of seeing you soon, for, God willing, after the feasts I shall leave Piacenza and stay 20 days in Florence. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. R.

1 The insolent letter is from the mother of Sr. A. Roberta Barbaglia. 2 On 18.12.77 Sr. A. Gesuina assures her that the Sister writes regularly to her relatives and that her last letter is dated 13 December.

She urges her to pay the rent and to make an enquiry on behalf of Fr Tor-natore.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. It would be good if you could pay the rent soon, because then the next half-year would come round, and it will certainly not look good.1

2. I have received the pictures, which are very beautiful; I tell you I did not expect so much.2 I hope (that) to be there with you within the month of January.3 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. ROSA

Best wishes to the Sisters. Goodbye, your affectionate M.

3. P.S. Listen, go to Fr Giuseppe, His Eminence's secretary,4 and

say to him: "The Father wishes to know whether he received a letter from him"; write

and tell me at once what he answers.

1 It would be good if you could pay the rent when the half-year falls due, be-

cause then the next one follows and it would not look good (bel vedere).

2 The pictures, a gift from Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi for the raffle. Cf. L 403,4.

3 She had told other Sisters too.

4 His Eminence Giuseppe Berardi, Cardinal Protector of the FSA.

She rejoices that the boarding school is going well. She tells her of her travels from early January. They will see each other again in Naples.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours and hear how well your boarding school is already going;1 blessed be God for it, who has so well formed my daughter's heart for me.

2. Listen, you want to know when I shall be in Rome;2 well, you must know that I am running a raffle for the house of the Morte,3 so I shall not be able to go to Rome until early January.

3. Besides, I shall have to stop along the way, so I shall reach Rome at the end of January, certainly not before.4

4. I shall be in Naples at the end of March and then I shall certainly see you, as it will be the good season then and you can come and see me, so we can talk of so many things; so take care of yourself and believe me ever your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 She wrote to her on 14 December that they have 4 boarders and hopes more will soon

enter. The possibility of giving piano lessons is being planned.

2 She wants to know when she will be in Rome because they have a box of lemons and ci-

trons, received as a gift, and want to send them.

3 Cf. L 403,4; 422, n. 2.

4 She wrote to Sr. A. Gesuina Moroni that she would stop in Florence. Cf. L 421,2.

She is worried about workmen being in the House in Via delle Fornaci. She asks her to invite the Sisters to stay with her over the Christmas holidays.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste. Listen, do me the kindness of going to the Fornaci unannounced.1 Oh! My God, you know, I am anxious about Sister A. Dorotea,2 because I hear there are men working there and I fear something may happen.

2. I am so worried; listen, have them come to you for these feast days and keep them there with you.3 Oh! What anguish I feel!

3. Be prudent and don't let them notice. Speak of it with the Superior without saying anything of what I am writing to you.4 For pity's sake, then, do everything you can, write to me and set my mind at rest.

Goodbye, your

affectionate M. R.

1 To the house in Via delle Fornaci.

2 Sr. A. Dorotea Benedetti.

3 The Superior Santina replies on 24.12: "Rest assured, I have already

told her; the Sisters of the Fornaci will spend these holiday days

at Margana".

4 In the same L she adds: "I told Superior Camilla and she did not realize

at all that it is an order from you".

She thanks them for the gifts received, but the finest

oro r

of all is the Sisters' resolution to observe the Holy Rules. News of her health.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have received all your gifts,2 and today so many others. I thank you and assure you that I was touched to see gifts raining on me from all sides.

2. Ah! My daughter, the finest of all is still the one you offer me in your letter, telling me that all the sisters made fervent resolutions to observe the Holy Rules.

3. Oh! My God, bless my dear daughters and make them all saints for me, so that one [day] I may have them with me in Paradise.3 I have received the rosaries. Goodbye, greetings to you all; in the Heart of Jesus I remain your affectionate

[M. R.]

4. P.S. I am writing to you on my knees because I am not very

well, and yesterday I spent Christmas (in) in bed, fainting again and again; I suffered

so very much; today I am up, but quite [weak]. Goodbye, your

[M. R.]

1 The date given is the 22nd, but in the P.S. she clearly says she is writing on 26

December.

2 Gifts for the raffle (cf. L 403,4) and for Christmas.

3 The finest... Paradise: the resolution of love and fidelity to the spirit of the Insti-

tute is the finest because it helps and supports her daughters along the way of

holiness and to continue in Paradise to be with her part of the Family

of the Holy Mother.

She has received her gift, an expression of genuine filial love, and thanks her, looking forward to their meeting in Naples.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter with 50 F. inside. Thank you, dear daughter. Oh! My God, it is very true that only the daughters born and raised in Mamma's lap1 are the ones who know their Mamma's needs.

2. So, dear daughter, what am I to say to you? Is a thank-you enough? And a word that tells you: We shall soon see each other? Are you pleased?2 The months fly, the days are shadows. So, until we meet in Naples and then in Piacenza. Yours

Affectionate M. ROSA GATTORNO

1 ...born and raised in Mamma's lap: these are the orphan daughters taken

in with motherly love in Piacenza, born and raised in the new family of

Mother Rosa and deeply devoted to her.

2 Are you pleased? She fully grasps the longing of this daughter, who in every let-

ter told her again that she wanted to see her.

Petition for reduced railway fares on the Romagna and Southern Lines for the journeys of the FSA Sisters for charitable purposes.

Your Excellency,

1. I, the undersigned, trusting in the kindness that moves Your Excellency's heart, appeal to you to obtain a favour. Before the Government handed over the Romagna and Southern line to the Railway Company, we, like the Sisters of Charity, enjoyed a 50% reduction on railway tickets, greatly to the benefit of our Institute,2 which, having as its purpose the instruction of children and the care of the sick in hospitals and, free of charge, in their homes, has to send its nurses travelling continually to the places where their work is most needed.

2. Once the railways had been handed over, the Company withdrew the fare reduction on the above lines both from us and from the Sisters of Charity, to our very grave loss. However, the Sisters of Charity, through the Honourable Mancini,3 recently obtained permission to enjoy this benefit once more.

3. Now I, in the name of this poor Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, petition Your Excellency to be so kind as to obtain that we too, since, having as our purpose the instruction and care of the sick, we work as far as our strength allows for the good of humanity, may enjoy the 50% reduction on railway tickets on the Romagna and Southern lines, so that we may more easily, because at less expense, hasten wherever we are called to serve.

4. I trust that Your Excellency, considering the above,

will kindly grant my petition; presenting my respects, I declare myself Your Excellency's

Most devoted Servant, signed Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Presumed to be from this period in view of the two following letters (L

428 and L 429), to which it seems to us to be linked, and of their context as regards

the correspondence of M. Rosa and Sr. A. Santina Solenghi.

2 Other requests for railway fare reductions have been published in Letters 3, L

184 and L 284.

3 The Honourable Minister Pasquale Stanislao Mancini.

She encloses the Minister's letter so that she can complete the procedure.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I enclose (a) the letter received from the Minister. Go at once; you see it depends on them? I would not like this talk of their having to wait for the Minister to be just an excuse.2

2. Tomorrow, God willing, they will leave, tomorrow at 9.3 I am in haste, your

Affectionate M. R.

P.S. For pity's sake be courteous with those people, do you understand me?

1 Cf. L 127, n. 1.

2 Perhaps Minister Pasquale Stanislao Mancini.

3 There is no further information to show whom she means.

She asks her to deliver a letter and tells her she is coming.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Take this letter at once to the Director of the Railways; now they have no more excuses; get them to give you the admission document,2 so I shall have the good fortune to be the first to travel at the reduced fare.

2. Goodbye. I shall come next week; you will be told by telegram.3

3. Goodbye; keep this letter with you, make a copy and take this one to them too, but do not leave it with them, do you understand? Leave them the copy - provided they do not take it amiss.

1 Cf. L 427, n. 1.

2 The document: the concession document.

3 Next week. She reached Rome in the first ten days of Jan-

uary 1878.

Indexes

I. FUNDAMENTAL THEMES OF THE SPIRITUALITY OF MOTHER ROSA GATTORNO

JOY. A constant disposition of serenity of spirit. "Be cheerful with dear Jesus".

II. INDEX OF THE RECIPIENTS OF THE LETTERS

1. AGOSTINI (Cardinal) DOMENICO. Born in Treviso on 1 June 1825, died in Venice on 31 December 1891. He studied at the episcopal Seminary of Treviso and the University of Padua. Ordained priest in 1851, he was curate to the parish priest of Santo Stefano in Treviso. He became esteemed as a preacher of "holy missions" in many parishes and towns of the Veneto. He was then pro-vicar general of the diocese and parish priest of Treviso cathedral. On 27 October 1871 Pius IX chose him as bishop of Chioggia and in 1877 promoted him patriarch of Venice. In 1882 Leo XIII created him cardinal of Venice. In 1876 he asked Mother Rosa Gattorno for FSA service in the diocese of Chioggia. The Foundress expressed her willingness (cf. L 211); on 13 July 1876 the Bishop replied that the matter should be deferred. AFSA CvIS, F58. There is no record of the project being taken up again. L 211.

2. BENTIVOGLIO (Countess) MATILDE, of one of the branches of the famous Bolognese family. She lived in Rome and, on the advice of the Mother President of the Tor de' Specchi Monastery, approached Mother Rosa for information on the Institute's activities, especially the nursing of the sick. The Mother replied at length in the letter published here. L 100.

3. BERARDI (Cardinal) GIUSEPPE. Born in Ceccano (Frosinone) on 28 September 1810. Having become a celebrated lawyer, he entered the judiciary. In 1844, after the untimely death of his wife and daughter, he took clerical dress. In 1851 he was appointed secretary for Extraordinary Ecclesiastical Affairs; he was also consultor of various congregations. In 1859 he became pro-secretary of state, in 1862 he was consecrated bishop and in 1868 created cardinal. From 1875 until his death on 6 September 1878 he was Protector of the Daughters of Saint Anne, maintaining excellent relations with Mother Rosa, whom he held in great esteem. To the FSA, especially the communities in Rome, he was a kind and attentive father. L 183.

7. CAPPONI (Bishop) FERDINANDO. Born in Florence on 1 April 1835. He was a doctor of theology at the University of his native city, then vicar general at Fiesole. He was sent as bishop to Volterra in 1874. He died on 21 March 1903. L 133.

10. CAVALLETTI (Marquis) FRANCESCO, husband of Maria Cavalletti Durazzo. He was a Senator in 1870; in 1874 he was among the supernumerary secret chamberlains of cape and sword. The Mother, having sent an important letter to his wife the Marchioness and fearing she was away from Rome, asked him to plead her cause. L 129.

11. CAVALLETTI (Marchioness) MARIA. Cf. Lettere 3, p. 733, one letter included. In this vol.: L 128.

12. CECCONI (Archbishop) EUGENIO. Born in Florence on 4 February 1834, died there on 15 June 1888. A student of the Capranica College, he obtained a doctorate in theology. Consecrated bishop in Rome on 3 January 1875, he governed the diocese of Florence from 1875 to 1888. In this vol.: L 23; 166; 178.

13. CENNI (Sr. A. Costanza) ZELINDA. Born at Galeata (FI) on 26 June 1849, she entered the Institute on 15 September 1873, introduced by the Jesuit Fr Alessandro Mancini. She received the religious habit on 30 September 1873. The Mother made her superior in various houses of the Institute: Rome - little Parish (school), Ovada (hospital), Varallo Pombia, Lodi, Trapani, Cosenza, Nico-sia. She testified as a witness in the Piacenza process on the virtues of the Servant of God Rosa Gattorno on 20 September 1913. She died

at Gargatano on 16.7.1928. Letters published in this vol.: 30.

14. COLLI (Teacher) ONORATA. Born on 25 May 1843, she died in Piacenza on 17 February 1912. She helped Mother Rosa from the first years of the foundation in Piacenza. "From 1869 to 1875 she taught with intelligence and zeal more than a hundred little orphans whom I took into this Institute. In this way she earned my high esteem and the affection of the poor girls she helped". So wrote the Foundress in a testimonial of 1895, stressing that this good teacher gave her services with dedication and free of charge. In school matters "Miss Colli" was the Mother's expert and prudent adviser, always ready to help, whether visiting a school to see how it was going and acting as intermediary with the school authorities, or preparing the Sisters for the teaching "diploma" examinations. At the Mother's request she wrote and edited the biographies of Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino and Sr. A. Francesca Camisa. She had known, loved and esteemed them both, as she knew, loved and esteemed many other FSA, especially the Mother's closest collaborators, Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega and Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, with whom she and her family kept up excellent relations even after Mother Rosa's death. She was also the Mother's secretary for the Institute's external affairs (cf. L 259). Over time the initial working relationship opened into the deepest and firmest friendship, extending affection and practical concern to both their families. Onorata took Carlotta to heart and was a sister, confidante and adviser to her; she introduced her into Piacenza's aristocratic society. Towards Alessandro she showed the most delicate attentions. She had understood his character and the goodness and sincerity of his soul, and so was able to help him in difficult times and plead his cause with the Mother herself. The Colli family welcomed him as one of the household during his stays in Piacenza. Mother Rosa was deeply grate-ful and returned her esteem and affection. L 55; 65; 169.

17. DI MARZO (Mgr) NICCOLA. Prelate of the papal Signatura of Justice, Protonotary and Consultor of the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars. He had recommended the FSA to the Commission of the "Opera Pia Granata" of Agrigento as a suitable Congregation to run the Orphanage, School and Boarding School of Agrigento, and had taken moral responsibility for the choice. His correspondence with Mother Rosa concerns precisely this matter. L 185; 224; 228.

20. FANTINI (Sr. A. Serafina) MARIA. Born in Rome on 2 July 1830, she entered the Institute as a widow at the age of 44. She received the religious habit on 30 May 1874. Given her age, ability and experience, the Mother made her Superior of the hospital community at Ovada in 1874 and two years later of the Sampierdarena hospital. She did not live up to this trust; on the contrary, she behaved as a stranger to the Family, to the point of ignoring and openly opposing the Mother's decisions regarding herself and the community, thereby putting the Mother in a bad light with the hospital authorities. She was dismissed from the Institute in October 1876. L 216.

21. FIOCCHI (Sr. A. Crocifissa) FELICITA, born on 10 September 1851 at Lizzano Belvedere (Bologna), daughter of Ignazio and Domenica Camparri. She entered at Ferrara, received by M. Rosa, who was there for the foundation of the house, introduced by Mgr Wanstien-kist, secretary to Cardinal Vannicelli. She received the religious habit on 8.12.1871. She did her first training nursing the sick in the Genoa House; she was then cook at Foligno in the early days of the foundation, then in Rome, at Tor de' Specchi and the little Parish. In 1878 the Mother made her superior of the Pistoia community and later sent her to open the house in Pisa (1879), then in Palermo (1881) at the Pignatelli Institute. She was superior for several years in Siena, where she died on 31 December 1935. In the AFSA in

21'

Rome 214 autograph letters from Mother Rosa addressed to her are preserved. The first two are published in this volume: L 365; 387.

22. GANDOLFI (Bishop) FRANCESCO. Born in San Remo (diocese of Ventimiglia) on 1 November 1812, he was preconized titular bishop of Antipatris. Transferred on 24 September 1868 to the diocese of Corneto and Civitavecchia. He died in Rome on 22 February 1882. L 310.

23. GARGA (Mgr) PIETRO. Born at Cesara, diocese of Novara, on 16 February 1822; died at Novara on 12 May 1889. Ordained priest on 21 December 1844, he was for many years secretary to the Bishop of Novara, Mgr Giacomo Filippo Gentili, and pro-vicar of the diocese. Consecrated bishop, he became his auxiliary and, on his death, his successor, in October 1875. L 158.

24. GASPARINI BRUTO, as mayor of Mer-catello, in the province of Pesaro, corresponded with Mother Rosa about the Sisters engaged by the Municipality for the girls' elementary school and the infant school. Relations were rather strained because of his insistence on applying to the religious, engaged under the Agreement with the Superior General, the legal rules for lay teachers, who were engaged in a personal capacity. This emerges from the Mother's letters to him in 1876, published here: L 213 and 219.

52. SCALABRINI (Bishop) GIOVANNI BATTISTA.

Born at Fino Mornasco (Como) on 8 July 1839, he died in Piacenza on 1 June 1905. He entered the seminary at Como after attending state schools; ordained priest in 1863, he was rector of the seminary from 1867 to 1870 and, after a brief spell as a parish priest, was appointed bishop of Piacenza in early January 1876. On that occasion Mother Rosa wrote him the first of a series of letters she would send him in the following years. His thirty years as bishop were marked by pastoral care and an enlightened openness to the social, cultural and religious realities of his time. He made the pastoral visitation of all 365 parishes twice and held three synods, one of them centred on Eucharistic worship. He strengthened the three diocesan seminaries and encouraged the founding at the Alberoni College of the "Divus Thomas" (1879), of which Fr Tornatore was one of the principal editors. In 1889 he held in Piacenza the first national catechetical congress, prepared by the review he had founded, "Il Catechista Cattolico". Having realized during his pastoral visits to the mountain parishes that many thousands of his diocesans were abroad for work, he twice went to America and, to care for them properly, founded the Missionaries, men and women, of St Charles. He turned to Mother Rosa, whom he held in great esteem, asking her for a directress and a novice mistress so that the new Missionary Sisters of St Charles might learn the "free and

modern spirit" of the Daughters of Saint Anne. In 1891 he wanted the FSA in New York for the first hospital founded by his Missionaries for emigrants. His cause for canonization is under way and the Decree on the heroicity of his virtues has been issued. L 170.
